name: Octagon House

lineage.note: Genuine blending. The octagon is a plan thesis with no ornamental vocabulary of its own, so nearly every built example wears Italianate dress: bracketed eaves, a cupola, round-arched windows, and a wrapping veranda.
The actual carpentry, trim profiles, and door and window stock of the earlier octagons are straight Greek Revival millwork; Fowler proposed a geometry, not a detail set.
Fowler's argument was explicitly against the rectangular house as wasteful of wall, of heat, and of steps, and against the classical box as an inherited habit nobody had audited.

description.short: An eight-sided house type promoted by the phrenologist Orson Squire Fowler in A Home for All (1848) on the argument that an octagon encloses more floor area per foot of wall than a rectangle, and adopted by several thousand American builders before it died of its own geometry.
description.long:
The octagon house is the only node in this branch that was generated by an argument rather than by a use, and it is therefore the most instructive one for anybody building a design system. Orson Squire Fowler was a phrenologist, a lecturer, a publisher of self-improvement literature, and an enthusiast of the sort the 1840s produced in quantity. His book A Home for All, or the Gravel Wall and Octagon Mode of Building appeared in 1848 and was reissued and expanded through the 1850s. Its case was quantitative and, as far as it went, correct: a regular octagon encloses about 21 percent more floor area than a square of the same perimeter, so it uses less wall for the same house; it presents more of its surface to sun and breeze; interior travel distances are shorter; and, in Fowler's second enthusiasm, it could be built by unskilled hands in lime-and-gravel concrete rather than in framed timber or laid brick. Several thousand were built between 1850 and 1860, concentrated in New York, New England, the upper Midwest, and Northern California.

It could not grow, and the reason is worth being candid about. Every economy Fowler identified is real, and every one of them is purchased by a geometric cost he did not price. Furniture, stairs, beds, tables, and rugs are rectangular, and human beings arrange rooms rectangularly; an octagon delivers its saved area as eight triangular residues in the corners, which become closets, or awkward passages, or nothing. Roof framing over eight hips converges on a point that wants to be a cupola whether the plan wants one or not. Additions are effectively impossible, because there is no elevation to extend without destroying the figure, and the American house of the period grew constantly. Within a decade the type was finished, not because taste turned but because the argument was incomplete.

That failure mode is exactly the one a kit-of-parts platform derived from first principles is exposed to. Fowler optimised a single legible metric, wall length per unit of enclosed area, and treated everything he had not measured as free. The traditional styles surrounding him in this taxonomy were optimised by nothing at all, only by two centuries of selection under real constraints, and they encode dozens of unstated accommodations to furniture, expansion, framing, weather, and habit that no closed-form argument recovers. A design system should be able to generate the octagon, because the octagon is real, and should also be able to say why almost nobody wanted a second one.

Inside a good one the experience is genuinely strange and rather pleasant. Light arrives from three or four directions in every principal room, so the quality of illumination is soft and shadowless in a way rectangular rooms of the period never achieve; the central stair rises to a cupola that pulls hot air out of the whole house in August, which was Fowler's other genuinely good idea; and the wrapping veranda means there is always a shaded side. What you cannot do is put a sofa against a wall without thinking about it, and that turns out to be enough.

defining_characteristics: A regular or near-regular eight-sided plan as the whole of the building's parti
A central vertical core, either a stair or a chimney stack, serving all eight sectors
A low eight-hipped roof converging on a flat deck or a cupola
A veranda or piazza wrapping a majority of the faces
Rooms arranged radially around the core, with triangular residual spaces used as closets, stairs, or service
Applied ornament borrowed wholesale from the prevailing style of the moment, usually Italianate, since the type supplies none of its own
diagnostic_tells: Eight exterior walls; there is no near-miss identification available
A cupola or belvedere at the roof apex, present in the large majority of surviving examples because the eight hips demand a termination
Wall construction is frequently lime-and-gravel concrete, board-formed in lifts, per Fowler's second thesis; look for horizontal form lines under the stucco
The ornament will date the house rather than the type, and it will almost always be Italianate bracketwork
Veranda runs continuously across five or more faces, breaking only at the entry

distinguished_from.difference: Nearly all octagons are Italianate in dress, so the two are not alternatives. Italianate is a style, the octagon is a massing thesis; a taxonomy that treats them as competing labels will misfile every surviving example.

Both are 1840s pattern-book propositions sold with a reformist argument, but Downing argued from feeling and moral influence and Fowler argued from arithmetic. The Gothic cottage is irregular by conviction; the octagon is regular by calculation.

proportional_system.governing_logic: Purely geometric, and uniquely so in this branch: a regular octagon, with everything else derived from the side length. The design is closed-form, which is both its appeal and its limitation.
typical_ratios: Side length 12 to 20 ft, giving an inscribed diameter of about 29 to 48 ft
Wall height 1.0 to 1.4 times the side length per storey
Cupola width 0.25 to 0.35 of the inscribed diameter
Veranda depth 7 to 10 ft, uniform on every face it crosses
Roof pitch 4:12 to 7:12 on all eight hips
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: One or two openings per face, identically placed on every face, producing an eightfold rotational rhythm with a single break at the entry.

massing_affinities.note: The type is the massing; there is no other reading.
Only as the central cupola or belvedere, never as an offset asymmetric tower.
The square-cored octagon with canted corners is a common cheat that gives up most of the geometric claim.
The octagon cannot be added to; picturesque growth destroys the figure that justifies the type.

constraints.statement: The plan shall be a regular octagon with all eight sides equal within 5 percent, side length between 12 and 20 ft. Irregular or elongated octagons forfeit the wall-economy argument that is the type's only justification.

A central core, being either the principal stair or a stack of flues, shall be provided and shall serve all storeys. Without it the eight-hip roof has nothing to bear on and the plan has no organising element.

No single room shall occupy more than three of the eight sides, and each principal room shall have openings on at least two faces. This is what buys the cross-light and cross-ventilation the type exists for.
A veranda shall run continuously across not fewer than five faces at a uniform depth of 7 to 10 ft, breaking only at the entrance face.

test.note: Tests the veranda-depth range. Coverage across not fewer than five of the octagon's eight faces, breaking only at the entrance, is a face-count-coverage fact with no matching variable and stays prose.

constraints.statement: Additions are prohibited on the primary figure. Where more space is required, build a detached or breezeway-linked wing; extending one face of the octagon destroys the type.

exemplars.name: Armour-Stiner (Octagon) House
exemplars.note: Built 1859-60 for Paul J. Armour on Fowler's principles; the encircling dome added and enlarged by Joseph Stiner 1872-76. The only known fully domed octagonal house.

exemplars.name: Longwood
exemplars.note: Samuel Sloan, designed 1859, construction halted by the Civil War in 1861 and never resumed above the basement storey. The largest octagonal house in the United States, and an Oriental-Italianate hybrid rather than a Fowler house.

exemplars.name: McElroy Octagon House
exemplars.note: Built 1860-61 by William C. McElroy at Gough and Union Streets; concrete construction, four rooms per floor around a central winding stair.

sources: Orson Squire Fowler, A Home for All, or the Gravel Wall and Octagon Mode of Building (1848; expanded 1853)
Carl F. Schmidt, The Octagon Fad (1958)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)
Marcus Whiffen, American Architecture Since 1780: A Guide to the Styles (1969)
